tagline: Follow the Russian River inland, then turn toward the Gravenstein Highway.
intro: Route 116 follows the Russian River’s north bank inland from Highway 1 near Jenner, then passes through Pocket Canyon toward Forestville. East and south of Forestville, rolling hills carry vineyards and apple orchards. Caltrans designates the stretch from Highway 1 to the Sebastopol city limit as a scenic highway. Redwood forests lie west of Forestville, with the Russian River to its north.

Guerneville’s railway connection to the San Francisco Bay ferries arrived in 1877. After train service ended in the late 1930s, vacationers continued coming to its resorts by automobile through the 1950s. At Sebastopol, the road’s modern shape followed a change in transportation: trains once ran along Main Street, but passenger service ended in the 1930s and regular freight service in the late 1970s. The tracks came out in the late 1980s. During that decade, Main Street and Petaluma Avenue became one-way streets to address traffic problems, reshaping the Gravenstein Highway through town.

Begin at Highway 1 and follow River Road east through Duncans Mills, Monte Rio and Guernewood Park to Guerneville. At the Guerneville Bridge intersection, Route 116 turns southeast toward Forestville through Pocket Canyon. It takes Front Street through Forestville, then turns south toward Graton and Sebastopol as Gravenstein Highway North.

moments.title: Duncans Mills
moments.text: Duncans Mills has an original railroad depot and cars, but one building’s old-fashioned appearance belongs to a later revival. Alexander Duncan established his sawmill here in 1877, sending lumber to San Francisco. The narrow-gauge North Pacific Coast Railroad ran through town, then ceased operating in the 1930s. A restoration project tied to the 1976 Bicentennial revived buildings and businesses. The State Park Sector Office looks like an original town building; it was actually part of that 1976 work. The community straddles Route 116 on the Russian River, about four miles from the Pacific.

moments.title: Guerneville
moments.text: Stumptown Days keeps Guerneville’s former English name in its annual parade. Logging in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries gave the place that name; demand for lumber rose after the 1906 earthquake and fires. The name Guerneville honors George Guerne, a Swiss immigrant who owned the town’s sawmill. Ancient trees survive in the Fife Creek watershed at Armstrong Woods Park, while the surrounding mountain forests include replacement plantings from the logging era. In the town center, a plaza with permanent chess tables provides a different landmark beside the river community’s forest history.

moments.title: Sebastopol
moments.text: Sebastopol’s annual Apple Blossom Festival in April and Gravenstein Apple Fair in August continue its connection to an orchard economy. Apples once brought steady prosperity, but competition from other growing regions reduced the industry’s economic importance in the second half of the twentieth century. Vineyards and housing replaced many orchards, and downtown lost its canneries and apple-processing plant. One part of the transport network found another use: the former Petaluma and Santa Rosa Railroad passenger depot houses the West County Museum, operated by the Western Sonoma County Historical Society. The railway’s stone powerhouse is also known as the Hogan Building.
